Alphabet watch list N (essay edition) So I didn't actually make it through this one, but I read the synopsis and still have thoughts. This movie has essentially the same premise as Gladiator, and it presents an interesting parallel. In Gladiator, the violence and evil has a purpose, and while it may not be fully historically accurate, the point is made and the emotions are evoked in the viewer. In the Northman, the violence and evil doesn't stop, and it seems to serve only to shock and disgust the viewer. It's dark and horrible just for the sake of being dark and horrible, and while that might work for somebody out there, I'm just not that person. I loved Gladiator because I could feel for Maximus and his struggle to avenge his family. Amleth is just angry and likes killing people. This movie probably isn't trying to be Gladiator or The Patriot, but for me those movies resonate in a way that this one misses the mark on.

I'm starting to think that the people who praise Eggers for historical accuracy are the same kind of people who think that photos are better than paintings because they "capture" the "reality" more precisely; that is to say: there is some perceived virtue in "depicting" the "past" as "accurately" as possible. I am sorry for all the quotation marks, but that's the quickest way to underline that all these ideas are... kind of dumb. I honestly don't care whether Eggers' movies are accurate and well-researched or not. It does not matter. There is so little intention behind the images on the screen that I can't bring myself to care about them. Also, the mask of "historical accuracy" kind of absolves the director of responsibility for any artistic decisions he makes; because, you see, that's how things were back then: violent, grey, boring, miserable. He's just showing things as true as possible! The weirdest part about the whole Eggers oeuvre for me is that I don't believe that he has any real interest or love for the eras he's depicting. It is paradoxical; he has built a reputation as this geek who is obsessed with the past, and yet it feels like they are just different Instagram filters for him. Puritanical 17th century New England? 19th century Germany? 10th century Scandinavia? Somehow, Eggers manages to make all of these look and feel the same. Ugh. We should all go read some Icelandic sagas (which are really fun and colourful and even humorous at times, by the way) instead of watching this.

I think the biggest consideration of period pieces is that their programming of speech and behaviour is of a time where different things were at stake, largely because ritual and power were at the forefront of the status quo, rather than, for an easy example, the possibility of the static lifestyle one can live now, of which human expedition then would ensure seriousness and expectation be within every walk of isolated thought and shared interaction. It’s against this backdrop that the opening stages’ questionable editing choices become most apparent: establishing that kind of world demands relaxation of a viewer’s experience through integration methods that are timeless in human history, and the film stumbles slightly out of the gate in giving us our footing. It is then the filmmaker’s job to ensure a universal entry point for even the most unintelligent of audience members to understand what is going on. Whilst it doesn’t contain the outstanding personality of The Lighthouse, instead here chasing spectacle in the traditional, predictable form (against its own intended “wow” factor) of “thing happens, get ready for next thing happening!! NEXT THING ARRIVES,” it does unquestionably provide the same fly-on-the-wall approach to that earlier work, giving us full spectator view of a meticulously designed production whose scale no one could argue with, and it’s here that the texture, where production design meets framing, makes a big bang. Where I’m less convinced is the camerawork itself. Eggers leans mechanical: constant pans, deliberate moves, in a way that keeps reminding you it’s camerawork rather than photography. These are undeniably seamless and the level of choreography required is evident in the final product, which is arguably perfect in achieving its intended circuitry (THE SEIGE!), yet there are moments that would’ve landed harder as a single, cleverly framed image of directed blocking, as a still image instead of motion for revelatory sake.

The commitment to realism with a pinch of fantasy is right up my alley. It’s just kind of boring and predictable, like watching someone play a video game you’ve already completed yourself. Con bellissimi paesaggi e una grande regia, che già dal primo minuto di visione si può già riconoscere chi lo ha diretto. Non parliamo poi della maniacale accuratezza storica che Eggers DEVE dare ai suoi film. I combattimenti che si vedono sono fantastici, e il come vengono mostrate certe scene: realistiche e crude, con il giusto quantitativo di violenza e una rappresentazione del periodo storico molto azzeccata. Il problema per me sta sopratutto nella storia che viene narrata, più che mai come viene narrata. La trama in sè, seppur non proprio all'apice dell'originalità, aveva una buona premessa. Essendo che c'era Eggers che lo scrive e dirige, mi faceva presagire già al mio nuovo film preferito. Invece no, dopo averlo finito mi sono sentito come ricevere un nuovo telefono solo per scoprire che all'interno c'è un mattone. Tutta la storia è strutturata con scene che portano avanti la trama, e sono divise da altre che servono a poco, con scene oniriche e piene di rituali ecc. Avendo visto anche the VVitch, era abbastanza prevedibile con Eggers, ma in questo caso non le ho viste come qualcosa che facesse parte della trama apparte qualche eccezione, come qualcosa che caratterizza il film e in molte occasioni non le ho trovate necessarie con il suo andazzo. Sopratutto nella seconda metà succede varie volte. Nonostante non sia un film horror, di soprannaturale ce ne è anche troppo. L'unico tocco di soprannaturale che ho gradito è il fatto che il Destino venga rappresentato come un'entità presente (come la morte in Final Destination ad esempio), se sia reale o solo un invenzione della capoccia del protagonista non lo sappiamo. Il Destino giuda Amleto per tutto il suo viaggio, anche quando cerca redenzione dalla sua vita piena di odio cercando di scappare da essa, il Destino torna e gli dice "Eh no, il tuo fato e già scritto, torna subito alla tua quest principale". Il finale, l'ho abbastanza gradito, anche se per il combattimento mi sarei aspettato tutt'altro epilogo, visto che per tutto il film il protagonista dice cosa farà una volta ottenuta vendetta. Per ora è il "peggior" film di Robert Eggers a mio parere.

If you asked me for my favorite revenge story, I'd have to give it to Berserk. I consider that manga to be a fantastic achievement and a shining example of what a revenge story could be. Berserk is a story that invites you to grow close to it's characters, to understand their desires, and to understand what they have to lose and what loss would mean to them. Upon the moment of betrayal, that seething hatred was something I felt on a visceral level. I was upset alongside the characters, and I was desperate (and still am) to see revenge take form. Comparing Berserk to The Northman is admittedly unfair. Comics, as a medium, can be much longer than movies. We're able to spend so much more time with the characters, and we're given a more intimate understanding of who they are. But what can I really say? I was ultimately disappointed with how little The Northman urged me to care about it's protagonist. It's a fairly familiar revenge plot (reminiscent of Hamlet) along the lines of "you killed my loved one; now I'll kill you". Protagonist vows to kill the man who "made his life hel", but you never get an understanding of what that misery looks or feels like to him. He is stoic, hyper-serious, and emotionally distant from the audience. None of this was aided by some non-sequitur side-questy sequences that were largely uninteresting. Don't get me wrong, the visuals are great. If all you want is brutality, it's in there. It's got a vibe of raw, primal hyper-masculinity through the filter of a psychedelic haze. It's actually pretty neat. Unfortunately the story is too unfocused and detached. Definitely my least favorite from Eggers. Pretty sure Willem Dafoe's character hangs dong, though, and that's cool.

The film looks great, and there is something here which could be a decently powerful story about lost innocence, a certain conceptualisation of masculinity/manhood, patriarchal violence unto women, a more metaphorical violence unto one’s identity, etc. The problem is that there’s basically no character work here. There is barely any humanity or life in this story which, on paper, should be very close to that humanity and life. I simply didn’t care about what was happening, especially with regard to the character relationships. As another user has already said, there’s also not much forward momentum: things just happen one after the other. The characters I most sympathised with were Olga and Gudrún, but that’s less because of their characters and more just because of the horrors they’re forced to endure with, by virtue of their status as women in such a patriarchal society, very little opportunity to do much about that. It’s probably the understated victimhood of the other characters - the ones who aren’t royal men - that the film gets to its most interesting themes (most notably the radical self-involvement/selfishness of the core character motivations that move the plot forward), but this is (seemingly intentionally) left as an understated part of the film and, even if it wasn’t, it wouldn’t counterbalance the issues I’ve already spoken about. I did want to like this film because I love Eggers’ work but this just didn’t work for me.

Not once does this movie stop to ask if you are ok. It forces you to accept Norse theology (although gruesome) in order to understand the characters. Even until the final scene, the movie does not once question the beliefs of those it is betraying. This makes the film feel like it is being told to you from a storyteller in 900 AD. That being said, one of the greatest rules of storytelling is broken. Amleth has no character arc, nor does he learn any sort of lesson. He is told at the beginning of his life what his fait is, and that is exactly what ends up happening to him. This feels natural, in fact the story wouldn't make sense if it were any other way. Amleth wouldn't truly be who he is portrayed as if it weren't for his adherence to his Norse ideologies. This got me thinking on The Oddesy. This story was told very differently and Odyseus almost feels out of place in his world. These two films represent the two different ways to tell an old story. The Oddysey is a modernized version of a story that feels relatable, while The Northman is a no-apologies telling of a story that stays honest (although not fully based on a historical story). It seems unfair to compare this to a Nolan film but boy does it hold its ground well.
